About me

I'm Naufal, an actuarial science graduate (S.Aktr.) from Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember in Surabaya. My training taught me not to avoid uncertainty but to measure it, and my thesis left me with one principle: no policy is perfect; there is only risk that is measured, reduced and mitigated.

At OJK East Java I saw what financial risk looks like for ordinary people, including small-business owners repaying online loans they never took because someone misused their identity. Since then I have wanted to work on the side that prevents those problems, not only the side that handles them afterwards.

Outside the models, I have spent three years leading teams and the data they rely on. Running the PKM database for 10,000+ students taught me that good decisions only come from data that is tidy, confidential and trusted.

How I work

I plan for missing data

No agency kept boat-loss records for the Bulak fishermen, so our survey plan was ready before the data requests came back empty. When the Surabaya office's claims for my thesis were incomplete, I went to the provincial office for the full 66 months.

I check a number two ways

Panjer recursion and FFT should give the same aggregate distribution, so I run both and measure the gap. The fishermen's premium went to an insurer's head actuary and an ITS academic before we used it.

I keep shared data tidy and private

The PKM database my division ran held records on 10,000+ students and their advisors. At OJK I handled credit-information requests and complaints that are confidential by design.

Aggregate loss, computed in your browser

Fit distributions to claims data, or pick them yourself. The page then builds the total loss twice, with Panjer recursion and with FFT, reads off VaR and TVaR, and prices it. The tail beyond VaR is marked in red.

Upload or paste claim sizes and claim counts; a sample is loaded to start with. The page fits twelve size and four count distributions by maximum likelihood, tests and ranks them, and the selected fits, the best by AIC unless you pick another, drive the model below. Your data never leaves your browser.

Claim sizes

One amount per claim, for example in rupiah. Zeros and negative values are ignored.

Claim counts

The number of claims in each period, for example each month. Whole numbers only.

Claim sizes

Claim counts

How the fitting works

Claim sizes: exponential, gamma, lognormal, Weibull, normal, inverse Gaussian, Pareto (Lomax), log-logistic, Burr XII, GEV, scaled beta (upper bound estimated as the largest value × (n + 1)/n) and a two-component lognormal mixture fitted by EM. Closed-form or Newton estimates are used where they exist, and Nelder–Mead on the log-likelihood otherwise.

Claim counts: Poisson, binomial (n by profile likelihood), negative binomial (r by profile likelihood) and geometric, tested with a chi-square test after merging cells with fewer than five expected periods.

Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-values use the asymptotic distribution, which is conservative when the parameters come from the same data. That is why the Anderson–Darling p-value can be bootstrapped: 199 samples are drawn from the fitted distribution, refitted and tested, as in my thesis.

Check: on my PKM 2025 survey data, this page reproduces the article: a binomial with n = 2 and p = 0.3656 for damage counts, and a lognormal with mean Rp169,064.29 for repair costs.

Choose a claim-count and a claim-size distribution below, or start from the pairs I selected in my thesis.

Premium principles compared

Conclusion and recommendations

Illustrative parameters: every claim-size distribution is scaled to a mean of 1 loss unit, and the presets reuse only the distribution families I selected for JKK and JKM, not my fitted values or any BPJS data. On the real claims, the two methods agreed to 5.37 × 10⁻¹⁷ before I backtested VaR and TVaR with the Kupiec test.

How the page computes this

Claim counts: binomial (q = 0.25, n = 4·E[N]), Poisson, negative binomial (r = 3) and geometric (r = 1). All four belong to the (a, b, 0) class, so Panjer recursion applies: fS(s) = [1 − a fX(0)]−1 Σj=1…s (a + bj/s) fX(j) fS(s − j).

Claim sizes, all with mean 1: gamma; Pareto (Lomax) with tail index above 2; Weibull; lognormal; GEV of the Fréchet type with shape below 0.5 and lower bound 0; beta with shapes (a, 2) scaled to [0, (a + 2)/a]; and a two-component lognormal mixture with component means in a 1 : 4 ratio.

Grid of 4,096 points (8,192 for heavier tails), rounding-method discretization; FFT with exponential tilting and four-fold padding. VaRp is the smallest grid loss with FS(s) ≥ p, and TVaRp = VaRp + E[(S − VaRp)+] / (1 − p).

Premium: twelve independent months of claims stay in the same (a, b, 0) family (Poisson with 12λ, binomial with 12n trials, negative binomial with 12r), so the annual distribution is built by FFT on a fine grid of up to 65,536 points. Pure premium = expected annual claims × (1 + inflation), discounted half a year at the investment return. Risk loading: cost of capital × (VaR or TVaR − expected claims), α × standard deviation, or θ × expected claims. Gross premium = (pure premium + risk loading) ÷ (1 − operating costs), shown per participant per month and as a share of the wage.

Comparisons: the moments of the exact distribution feed three classic approximations, the normal, the translated gamma (matching mean, variance and skewness) and Normal Power, and a Monte Carlo of 100,000 periods draws claim counts and claim sizes from the same discretised distributions. Premium principles: the Wang transform prices claims under the survival curve shifted by λ standard normal units, Φ(Φ⁻¹(S(x)) + λ), and the Esscher transform under weights proportional to exp(h × claims).

Managing the fund

  1. Liquidity first. Claims must be paid within days, so keep at least the liquid amount above in instruments you can withdraw quickly: sharia savings, short sharia time deposits or a sharia money market mutual fund.
  2. The investment share goes to low-risk sharia fixed income, such as government retail sukuk (the SR and ST series) or a sharia fixed-income mutual fund, ideally with something maturing every year.
  3. No individual stocks for the tabarru' fund. Prices can fall in the same year claims spike, and a forced sale would lock in the loss. Members who want equity exposure can invest their returned surplus personally.
  4. Check every product is registered with and supervised by OJK, and buy through a bank or a registered selling agent (APERD).
  5. Govern it openly: separate accounts for tabarru', ujrah and investment, two signatories from the KUB, and a monthly report to members.

Educational illustration, not investment advice. Returns are assumptions you can change above.

How the calculator works

Damage rate per boat = events ÷ boats observed × risk factors; the kelurahan factor also scales the average repair cost by what the PKM survey observed there. Repair costs follow a lognormal distribution with the average and spread you enter, capped at the boat value; a total loss pays the boat value. Pure premium = expected repair cost per boat a year. The tabarru' share is the pure premium plus the safety margin; contribution = tabarru' share ÷ (1 − ujrah − investment share). With PKM's numbers (E[N] = 0.7312, E[X] = Rp169,064.29, 75 / 10 / 15 split) this gives Rp164,822.53 a year, or Rp13,735.21 a month.

The group's annual claims are computed exactly with FFT on a fine grid: binomial counts with at most two events per boat (or Poisson), lognormal repair costs and optional total losses. Fake claims add extra claims that verification fails to catch. The minimum group size is the smallest number of members for which the chance of a short year stays within your target. The 5-year projection samples 2,000 paths from that distribution and follows PKM's surplus rule: 40% back to members, 25% to the KUB as manager and 35% to collective savings, which absorbs short years together with the investment pot.

Claim models compared: the same expected events and repair cost, run through the same FFT with Poisson or negative binomial (r = 2) event counts, and with gamma or Weibull repair costs matched to the same mean and coefficient of variation.

Technical provisions at launch

Capital: the deterministic RBC rule against a stochastic 1-in-200 year

How the model works

Expected claim cost E(c) = p(sick) × daily benefit × days + p(death) × death benefit + p(disability) × disability benefit + p(sick) × handling cost; the COD rider adds p(failure) × deliveries × value. Gross premium = (1 + administration + risk margin) × E(c) ÷ (1 − commission − other expenses − profit).

Technical provisions at launch, the Bornhuetter–Ferguson starting point before any claims have developed: unearned premium (UPR) = premium × policies; expected ultimate loss (EUL) = E(c) × policies; IBNR = a share of EUL; outstanding claims (OCR) = EUL + IBNR; catastrophe buffer = a share of OCR; total (TTP) = UPR + OCR + buffer.

Projection: policies × (1 − lapse) × (1 + growth) a year; net cash flow = premium − operating cost − claims; capital = target RBC × TTP, with TTP following the policies in force. Present values use the discount rate, and the break-even year is when cumulative net cash flow first covers the year-1 capital.

Stochastic check: the year-1 counts of sick spells, deaths, disabilities and failed cash-on-delivery parcels are drawn from binomial distributions over 20,000 simulated years, optionally with a 15% lognormal uncertainty on every claim rate; the capital for a 1-in-200 year is the 99.5% quantile of claims minus premiums net of operating costs.

Methods compared

Same region, soil, ground-motion model and simulations as above; each row changes one modelling choice.

Conclusion and recommendations

How the model works

Hazard: the USGS catalog of 701 earthquakes around the Sunda Strait is converted to moment magnitude and declustered with Gardner–Knopoff-type time and distance windows, leaving the mainshocks. Each mainshock keeps its place and depth (interface up to 50 km, intraslab below), and its magnitude is redrawn from a generalized Pareto distribution fitted by maximum likelihood to the magnitudes above the threshold. My notebook kept 303 mainshocks; events with equal magnitudes are ordered differently here, which leaves 301, and the GPD fit is the same.

Ground motion and damage: for every draw, spectral acceleration at the regency office is computed with Atkinson and Boore (2003), Zhao et al. (2006) and BC Hydro (2012) at each building type's period (PGA, 0.3 s or 0.6 s), and averaged as in the project. GEM vulnerability curves turn it into a loss ratio for each of the building types in the residential inventory, multiplied by their replacement value. Each event's loss is computed exactly on a 161-point magnitude grid and read off for every draw.

Annual loss: every mainshock recurs as a Poisson process with rate 1 / ARI, and its loss is drawn from a Gaussian kernel density of its simulated losses (Scott's bandwidth), over 2,000 simulated years. VaR and TVaR come from a zero-inflated lognormal fitted to the annual losses, as in the notebook, and the figures read straight from the simulation are shown beside them.

Method options: the frequency can follow the catalog, where 12 mainshocks above Mw 5.8 in 50.5 years give 0.24 a year, instead of one occurrence of every event per ARI; ground motion can include each model's aleatory variability (σ), as probabilistic hazard studies do; magnitudes can follow a truncated Gutenberg–Richter law with the catalog's b-value; and event losses can be resampled directly instead of through a Gaussian kernel, which adds symmetric noise to skewed losses.

Equity risk lab

Load daily closing prices for up to five stocks and the page measures their risk: Value at Risk and Tail Value at Risk at 90%, 95% and 99% by three methods, a rolling Kupiec backtest, the minimum-variance and maximum-Sharpe portfolios, CAPM betas against an index, simulated price ranges and a long-term pension plan. It grows out of my VaR project on agribusiness stocks and my corporate finance project on a pension fund.

For learning, not investment advice. Comparisons mean most when the stocks share a sector; the page cannot check that for you.

What a price file looks like

A date and a closing price, one row per trading day. Files exported from Investing.com (Indonesian or English) and Yahoo Finance work as they are: the page reads Tanggal and Terakhir, Date and Price, or Date and Close. Save Excel files as CSV first.

Returns

Value at Risk and Tail Value at Risk

The portfolio by seven methods, with a backtest

Kupiec's test checks one-day VaR forecasts made from a rolling 250-day window: how often the loss went past VaR, against how often it should have.

Christoffersen's test adds a check that those days do not come in clusters; a method passes when both tests hold at both levels.

Portfolio weights

Weights estimated on the first half, held through the second

CAPM against the index

Simulated price ranges

Pension plan

Monthly contributions split between the chosen stock portfolio and fixed income, rebalanced every month. Each stock month is a random 21-day block of the portfolio's past returns.

Conclusion and recommendations

How the lab computes this

Daily log returns from closing prices, on the dates every loaded series shares. Historical VaR and TVaR read the empirical loss distribution (overlapping sums for 10 days); Normal uses the mean and standard deviation; Student-t fits location, scale and degrees of freedom by maximum likelihood and simulates 10,000 outcomes. A loss is 1 − eR of the value, so it never exceeds 100%.

Portfolios are rebalanced daily. The minimum-variance and maximum-Sharpe portfolios are long-only and found exactly by checking every subset of stocks. CAPM beta is the slope of each stock's daily return on the index's; the CAPM return is rf + β × (index return − rf). Kupiec's proportion-of-failures test uses a chi-square with one degree of freedom.

Check: on my project's TBLA, LSIP and SMAR prices, the minimum-variance portfolio puts 53.1% in SMAR, against 53.5% in the original analysis.

More methods: Cornish–Fisher adjusts the normal quantile for skewness and excess kurtosis; EWMA (RiskMetrics) weights recent days more, with λ = 0.94; GARCH(1,1) is fitted by maximum likelihood and its standardised residuals are resampled (filtered historical simulation), matching scipy's estimates; extreme value theory fits a generalised Pareto distribution to the worst 10% of daily losses. In the rolling backtest GARCH is refitted every 20 days and the tail every 5. Christoffersen's test checks that breaches are independent; Ledoit–Wolf shrinks the covariance towards a scaled identity, and risk parity gives each stock an equal share of the portfolio's volatility.

Forecasting lab

From my Financial Forecasting Methods projects and my ARIMA coursework. Load a series and the page holds back its last stretch, fits naive benchmarks, Holt-Winters and an ARIMA chosen by AIC, scores each one on the held-back data, then forecasts ahead with 80% and 95% intervals.

Conclusion and recommendations

How the lab works

Benchmarks: the naive forecast repeats the last value, the seasonal naive repeats the value from one season earlier, and the drift forecast extends the line from the first to the last point. A model is only useful if it beats them on data it has not seen.

Holt-Winters: additive exponential smoothing with a level and, where they help, a plain or damped trend and a seasonal pattern; the variant with the lowest AIC is kept. Theta: simple exponential smoothing with half the slope of a linear trend as drift, on seasonally adjusted data, as in the M3 forecasting competition; it matches statsmodels' ThetaModel. ARIMA: the number of regular differences comes from a KPSS test and the seasonal difference from the strength of seasonality, then every ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q) with p and q up to 2 and P and Q up to 1 is fitted by conditional sum of squares on a common sample, kept stationary and invertible, and the lowest AIC wins; on the daily Delhi series, ARIMA(0,1,3) matches statsmodels to three decimals. The combination averages the ETS, ARIMA and Theta forecasts, which often beats each of them.

Each model is fitted to everything before a test window and scored with RMSE, MAE and MAPE. When the series is long enough this is repeated on the last three windows (a rolling origin), and the lowest average RMSE wins, which is steadier than a single window. The winner is refitted to the full series for the forecast. Intervals assume normal errors; with the logarithm option, forecasts and intervals are transformed back. The Ljung–Box test checks whether the best model's residuals still hold autocorrelation.

Conclusion and recommendations

How the lab works

Data: the sample is a public auto-insurance dataset of 1,000 claims with real fraud labels, 24.7% of them fraudulent. Categories become one-hot columns, numbers are standardised on the training claims, and the split keeps the fraud rate equal in training and testing. SMOTE creates synthetic frauds from the training claims only, so the test claims keep the real fraud rate.

Models: logistic regression with an L2 penalty fitted by Newton's method, a CART decision tree on Gini impurity, Gaussian naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours, a linear SVM with squared hinge loss solved by dual coordinate descent, a random forest of 100 trees and gradient boosting with 150 shallow trees, the last two on histogram bins as in LightGBM. On the same split, the first five match scikit-learn's ROC-AUC within 0.003 and the two ensembles within 0.006.

Judging: ROC-AUC is the chance that a random fraud scores above a random honest claim, and PR-AUC summarises precision against recall. For money, claims are flagged from the highest score down; every caught fraud saves the chosen share of its claim amount and every flag costs one investigation. The threshold that saves the most is found on the test claims, so it is a little optimistic. Five-fold cross-validation repeats the training on five different splits, which shows how much a score owes to the luck of one split.

Automatic summary

How the lab works

Columns are read as numbers when at least 90% of their filled cells are numeric, in either 1,234.5 or 1.234,5 style; other columns are treated as categories. Quartiles and percentiles use the same rule as Excel's PERCENTILE.INC and R's default, skewness and excess kurtosis match Excel's SKEW and KURT, and the standard deviation and variance are sample values.

Normality: the Shapiro–Wilk test follows Royston's algorithm, the one in R and scipy, for 3 to 5,000 values, and the Jarque–Bera test uses the sample skewness and kurtosis. Outliers are values beyond 1.5 or 3 interquartile ranges from the quartiles. Correlations use the rows where both values are present, and density curves use a Gaussian kernel with Silverman's bandwidth.

On the sample data, every statistic here, including the Shapiro–Wilk W, matches numpy and scipy to at least four decimals.
